title: Spider bites and scorpion stings: what to do

answer: Most spider bites and scorpion stings cause only mild symptoms, but severe toxicity and death can occur.
Watch first for a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis): it is the most concerning initial effect and must be recognized and treated immediately.
Care is mainly supportive: wound care and pain control. Most scorpion stings can be adequately managed with pain medicine such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen and routine wound care.
After a scorpion sting, observe the person for 4 to 6 hours to make sure no symptoms come on late.

Black widow (the female is black with a red hourglass-shaped mark on the abdomen): the bite may or may not be felt as a pinprick, and the bite site is often not found. Painful muscle cramping starts at the bite and moves toward the center of the body, typically beginning 15 to 60 minutes after the bite, and the abdomen may become painful and rigid. Bites are rarely fatal, but medical attention is still recommended.

Brown recluse: within several hours there is pain, itching and swelling; a blister or a central purple area forms and can become an ulcer, sometimes not until days later. Treatment is wound care and relief of pain and itching; there is no antivenom.

Scorpion: a painful sting, often with tingling or burning. There can be irritability and agitation; in severe cases, seizures and a high body temperature. Infrequently, severe muscle spasm can compromise the airway and stop breathing.

Australian funnel-web spider (severe and potentially fatal): wrap the bitten limb with an elastic bandage, tight enough to limit spread but not to restrict blood flow, take the person to the nearest medical facility with the bandage in place, and do not remove the bandage until antivenom is ready to be given.

If bitten by a spider and experiencing severe symptoms, seek immediate medical attention. For severe or progressive symptoms after any spider bite or scorpion sting, get the person evacuated early to a facility that can give advanced care.
warnings: Scorpion sting: do not apply a tourniquet, do not burn (cauterize) the sting, and do not cut it open.
Brown recluse bite: early cutting out of the bite is not indicated. An expanding area of dead tissue, or fever, weakness, vomiting or joint pain, needs admission to a medical facility.
Most severe and fatal scorpion envenomation occurs in children under the age of 10.
After any bite or sting, tetanus protection should be checked by medical personnel.

quotes.text: While most spider and scorpion envenomations result in mild symptoms, severe toxicity and death can occur.

Unlike other types of injuries, patients may not even recognize they were envenomated by arthropods, as many injuries are painless or felt as a pinprick. Anaphylaxis is the most concerning initial eﬀect. Recognize and treat it immediately using standard acute allergic reaction therapies.
For all bites/stings, assess tetanus status and administer vaccine and/or immunoglobulin (for those not previously immunized against tetanus) if required.
Multiple species of widow spiders (Latrodectus spp.) are found on various continents (North America, Asia, Europe, Africa, and Australia).
Patients may or may not feel a pinprick upon the initial bite. A pair of small red spots at the envenomation site may be visible. However, the bite site is often not located.

Some patients do not develop systemic toxicity. In those patients who do, symptoms typically begin 15 to 60 minutes following the envenomation. The primary symptom is painful muscle cramping, starting at the bite site and progressing towards the center of the body. Patients may develop a painful, rigid abdomen secondary to abdominal muscle spasm which may be mistaken for peritonitis.
Treatment consists primarily of supportive care, pain management, and wound care (to include tetanus prophylaxis). Given the low risk of infection, antibiotics are not routinely recommended.

The Black Widow Spider is found in various parts of the world. Females have a distinctive black body with a red hourglass-shaped mark on the abdomen. Their venom contains neurotoxins that can cause intense pain, muscle cramps, nausea, and in severe cases, can affect the nervous system. While bites are rarely fatal, medical attention is still recommended.

The Brown Recluse Spider is found primarily in the U.S. Their bites can cause tissue necrosis (cell death), leading to an ulcerous wound that may require medical attention. Other symptoms can include pain, itching, and systemic effects.
Loxosceles reclusa in a venomous spider more commonly known as the brown recluse, violin spider, or ﬁddleback spider.

Loxoscelism will present as an ulcerative lesion, sometimes not until days after the initial envenomation. In general, within several hours after the initial bite there will be local ischemia resulting in pain, pruritus, and swelling. A blister or a central area of purple discoloration will form.

Treatment of local symptoms includes wound care, tetanus prophylaxis, analgesics, and antipruritics as necessary. There is no antivenom available. Early excision, intralesional injection of corticosteroids, and dapsone are not indicated.
Systemic loxoscelism manifestations include fever, weakness, vomiting, joint pain, petechiae, rhabdomyolysis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and hemolysis.
Patients with an expanding necrotic lesion or symptoms of systemic loxoscelism should be admitted to a medical facility.
Scorpion stings produce a painful local reaction often including the sensation of tingling or burning.
Sympathetic stimulation via excess catecholamine release produces hypertension, tachycardia, irritability, and agitation. In severe cases, patients may develop seizures and hyperthermia.
While infrequent, severe muscle spasm can result in airway compromise and respiratory arrest.

The majority of scorpion envenomations can be adequately managed with pain medications (ibuprofen, acetaminophen, and opioids) and routine wound management to include tetanus prophylaxis. Most patients, especially adults, will not develop signiﬁcant symptoms. Patients should be observed for 4-6 hours after envenomation to ensure no delayed onset of symptoms. Prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated. Application of a tourniquet, cauterization, and incision and drainage are contraindicated in scorpion stings.
The majority of severe and fatal envenomation occurs in children under the age of 10 due to their decreased body mass.
Australian funnel web spiders are capable of inducing a severe and potentially fatal neurotoxic envenomation syndrome.

Prehospital management consists of pressure immobilization using an elastic crepe bandage applied tightly enough to limit lymphatic spread, but not to restrict blood ﬂow. The venom of the funnel web spider is one of the few animal venoms to undergo local inactivation. The patient should be transported to the nearest medical facility with the bandage in place, and the bandage should not be removed until antivenom is readily available to be administered.

Evacuation to facility capable of advanced supportive care (i.e. intubation, mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, antivenom) will be considered early for severe or progressive symptoms, including Grade 3 or 4 scorpion envenomation.

While these spiders are considered dangerous, actual bites and severe reactions are relatively rare. Most spiders are not aggressive and will only bite in self-defense. If bitten by a spider and experiencing severe symptoms, seek immediate medical attention.
